overview: I2103 combines the low-altitude approach maneuver with the instrument recovery skills that keep an avionics or attitude problem from becoming a loss-of-control problem. Be ready to brief the profile, recover unusual attitudes by instruments, and transition to BFI/IAC failure procedures without rushing away from aircraft control.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: The approach maneuver simulates a low-altitude instrument approach from over a NAVAID while forcing clean scan, timing, descent control, BAC transition, and missed-approach discipline.

children.text: Start at 200 KIAS in straight-and-level flight on a cardinal heading.
Slow toward 150 KIAS with about 15% torque; anticipate left rudder and trim right rudder plus up elevator as the aircraft decelerates.
Approaching 150 KIAS, add power to about 33% to maintain level flight and re-trim.
Turn right standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB, for 90 degrees of heading change while maintaining altitude and using the one-third rollout rule.
After the 90-degree turn, start the clock for two minutes, set about 15% torque, and descend 1000 feet at 150 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
About 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 33% and level at 150 KIAS.
At the end of two minutes, begin a left standard-rate turn for 210 degrees; anticipate a small need for power and back-stick pressure to hold level flight at 150 KIAS.
After the 210-degree turn, slow down first, then go down: reduce power to about 15% and maintain altitude to expedite deceleration.
Below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, set flaps to T/O, and execute the Before Landing Checklist.
At 120 KIAS, lower the nose and descend 1000 feet; about 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 42% to maintain 120 KIAS.
Stabilize on altitude and heading, reset the clock, set about 15% torque again, and descend another 1000 feet at 120 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
At the end of the second two-minute timing segment, execute the missed approach: max power, right rudder, and 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Check VSI and altimeter, call two positive rates and raise the gear; above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps.
Report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS, then set 8 to 10 degrees nose high and accelerate toward 180 KIAS while climbing 2000 feet.
Start the 200 KIAS cruise transition about 200 feet before level-off.
The maneuver is complete at 200 KIAS, on the heading used after the 210-degree turn, and 1000 feet below the original starting altitude.

The event's special navigation requirement is to proceed direct to homefield using an available NAVAID when directed; brief the navigation method as part of the approach setup, not as a separate discussion item.
Common errors are late power changes, poor trim through BAC, chasing rate with pitch instead of power, and missing gear/flap cleanup during the missed approach.

items.text: IFR unusual-attitude recovery is an instrument scan and verification problem: recognize the bad attitude, confirm it against backup/performance instruments, and recover without creating a worse energy state.

children.text: An unusual attitude is any unexpected or inadvertent attitude encountered during normal instrument flight.
To avoid the situation in IMC, roll should normally be limited to 30 degrees AOB, nose low to 10 degrees, and nose high to 15 degrees.
Common causes include slow scan, spatial disorientation, fixation on a subtask, and transition from VFR to IFR.
Recognize with attitude indicator and performance cues, then confirm actual attitude with the BFI and performance instruments before recovering.
Relax back-stick pressure while maintaining positive G so the nose can fall toward the horizon.
Roll toward, but not past, 90 degrees of bank; use only as much bank as needed.
If climbing, use power as required to keep airspeed above stall.
As the miniature aircraft approaches the horizon, adjust bank toward wings level; if airspeed is below 100 KIAS, the nose may continue below the horizon until safe flying speed is restored.
Roll wings level first.
Start the pull only after the wings are level.
Approaching 200 KIAS or greater, reduce power and use speed brake if required to stay below maximum allowable airspeed.
Recovery is complete when the aircraft is back in the desired attitude for normal instrument flight.
Common nose-high errors are pushing negative G, not rolling enough toward 90 degrees when needed, and failing to add power.
Common nose-low errors are pulling before wings level and forgetting to reset power or speed brake after recovery.

items.text: In I2103, IMC emergency thinking is tied directly to unusual attitudes and avionics failures: stabilize first, then troubleshoot.

children.text: Use the NATOPS emergency priorities: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation and take proper action, then land as soon as conditions permit.
Critical action memory items are completed immediately when required; time permitting, back them up with the checklist.
In IMC, protect altitude, attitude, terrain clearance, and ATC coordination before local convenience or troubleshooting flow.

For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or an IMC abort, maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit.
Squawk and declare as required, tell ATC your intentions, and avoid a heads-down troubleshooting posture until the aircraft is stable.
If the emergency is an avionics failure, transition to the BFI or remaining reliable instruments before touching repeat switches or circuit breakers.

items.text: Dual IAC failure is an avionics-failure event that can remove the normal flight-display picture; the first answer is to fly the aircraft from backup references before troubleshooting.

children.text: Dual IAC failure results in loss of HUD, UFCP, and MFD displays in both cockpits.
A single IAC failure may not show an IAC failure message, but may cause MFD loss in one or both cockpits, erratic MFD behavior, HUD or UFCP malfunction, or synchronization errors.
Synchronization errors can show up as mismatched heading, altitude, or airspeed bugs between cockpits, QNH DISAGREE on the FMS, or incorrect REPEAT-mode behavior.
If synchronization errors or erratic indications are detected on the ground, takeoff is not recommended.
If synchronization errors exist without MFD loss, do not select REPEAT in either cockpit.
Do not select REPEAT from a cockpit with working MFDs during suspected crosstalk or synchronization failure; it may lead to loss of all MFD information in both cockpits.
Reference the BFI as required.
Set the NORM/REPEAT switch to NORM in both cockpits.
Check IAC1 and IAC2 circuit breakers on the left and right front console and reset if open.
If IAC/MFD failures or erratic displays persist, pull the failed IAC circuit breaker or breakers, then reset after 5 seconds.
If failures, erratic displays, or synchronization errors persist, land as soon as practical.

items.text: The BFI is the backup attitude and performance reference that keeps the aircraft flyable after PFD, ADC, IRU, or IAC failures.

children.text: The BFI is in the upper right side of the instrument panel in both cockpits.
It provides attitude, altitude, airspeed, heading, and vertical velocity.
It is normally powered by the battery bus; with a battery-bus failure, the auxiliary battery can power it through the AUX BAT switch.
The front cockpit circuit breaker is STBY INST; rear cockpit BFI power is through AFT STBY on the front-cockpit panel.
The adjustment knob changes baro; pushing it sets STD 29.92.
The M push-button enters or exits menu mode.
Useful menu items include FAST ERECT, SET BRIGHTNESS, FAST ALIGN, and SET HEADING when no external heading data is available.
FAST ERECT requires straight-and-level, non-accelerated flight.
If the PFD is partly or fully lost, reference the BFI, smoothly level the wings with coordinated rudder and aileron, and set the nose to straight-and-level attitude.
Once the aircraft is stabilized, complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure.
The common error is rushing into an emergency procedure before the aircraft is stabilized in straight-and-level BFI flight.
ATT FAIL removes pitch ladder, roll pointer, and slip/skid while leaving roll scale and aircraft symbol on a cyan background.
Processor errors may show as a red X or a black screen with instructions.

studyNotes.summary: Fly the approach maneuver precisely, then show that unusual attitudes, IMC emergencies, IAC failures, and BFI-only flight all start with the same control-first instrument discipline.

summary: Approach maneuver execution, instrument-only recovery, dual IAC failure, and BFI control.
title: Approach Maneuver
